description:
Market Window Dossier gives teams dated evidence and a checklist for planning launch timing before development and reviewing freedom to operate (FTO). It is not an FTO or legal opinion. LOE-Bench is an observational benchmark based on regulatory records. It tests how well different forecasts place drugs that later receive a first final US generic approval in a fixed 20% review queue. At each forecast date (the cutoff), reviewers can check one in five eligible cases, rounded down. An eligible case is a US small-molecule drug with a documented new molecular entity approval and no first final generic approval by that date. The outcome is the FDA's first final approval of an original Abbreviated New Drug Application (ANDA) within 12 or 24 months after the cutoff. Commercial launch, time saved by reviewers, Thai demand and freedom to operate each require separate evidence.

Forecasts and primary comparisons

We compare three forecasts on the same cases. B1 uses time since the original approval. M1 adds information such as listed patents, exclusivity and recorded patent challenges. M3 adds a graph that summarizes this evidence as OPEN, BLOCKED or CONTESTED. OPEN refers to the graph's rules for interpreting the records and gives no freedom-to-operate clearance. For each model, we count the cases in the review queue that later receive a first final generic approval. We first compare M3 with B1 at 24 months. If that test succeeds, we compare M3 with M1 at 24 months. If the second test also succeeds, we compare M3 with B1 at 12 months. These tests quantify how many approvals each queue captures. They do not estimate reviewer benefit or causal effects.

Historical and prospective evaluation

Track C′, the historical analysis, uses Orange Book editions we can verify were available at each scheduled cutoff. After OSF registration, the analysis lead checks that every required edition is available and that at least 50 distinct drugs received their first final ANDA approval in an eligible 24-month window. If either check fails, the historical hypotheses remain untested, and we report what prevented evaluation. Earlier work reported aggregate baseline results from overlapping historical periods. Knowledge of Data explains which outputs were generated, who inspected them and how they were used.

For Track A, the prospective analysis, we use the 27 November 2026 source snapshot and freeze predictions before retrieving later outcome records. We will hash and tag the predictions and add them to OSF before 31 January 2027 at 23:59 UTC. The 12- and 24-month windows end on 27 November 2027 and 27 November 2028. The prospective analysis has a separate family of tests. Track A is confirmatory if Track C′ was not run as a confirmatory analysis. If Track C′ was run as confirmatory, Track A is a replication regardless of the historical results. B3 uses expiry dates alone and is a secondary comparator. Eligible forecasts from the large language models (L1 and L1e) and the C9 comparison of group relative policy optimization (GRPO) with supervised fine-tuning are exploratory if they satisfy the protocol requirements. Track B describes biologics.

Interpretation

We report whether the gain reaches ten percentage points. In simulations with 75 event drugs, we detected a gain of that size about half the time. The development results motivate testing how cases are prioritized for review. Cases outside a queue still follow the usual review process. The development analyses did not establish that any arm could safely clear cases automatically.

How queue performance is measured

At each cutoff, rank every eligible case by its model's unrounded native risk score and put the highest-scoring fifth in the review queue, rounding the slot count down. If a tie straddles the last slot, give every tied case an equal chance to fill one of the remaining slots. For each year, count how many drug groups with an upcoming first final approval enter the review queue. If four groups tie for two remaining places, each receives half credit. Add the credits across years and divide by the total number of drug-year observations with an upcoming approval. One approval can qualify at two annual cutoffs. That fraction is queue recall. Queue precision divides the same expected hits by the number of slots. To calculate distinct event-drug capture, use independent tie lotteries across cutoffs, calculate each event drug's chance of appearing in the queue at least once on a positive row, and average those chances across event drugs.
